documents.excerpt: When God confronts, corrects, disciplines, or crushes a person, in which direction does the spirit break?
excerpts: When God confronts, corrects, disciplines, or crushes a person, in which direction does the spirit break?

A wrong spirit breaks away into defensiveness, blame, bitterness, anger, performance, hiding, or despair; a right spirit breaks toward God in confession, humility, dependence, surrender, praise, and hope.
A right spirit is not one that never breaks—everyone’s spirit will break—but one that breaks in the right direction.

documents.excerpt: Elijah states the principle: the sin one makes peace with today can become the sin that masters tomorrow; the useful question is where present compromises are leading.
excerpts: Elijah states the principle: the sin one makes peace with today can become the sin that masters tomorrow; the useful question is where present compromises are leading.

Private choices form desires. Kept boundaries strengthen the next boundary, while moved boundaries make later movement easier; affairs begin with messages, hidden conversations, repeated looks, and welcomed attention.
Quoting John Owen, Elijah urges believers to be killing sin rather than accommodating, renaming, negotiating with, or keeping it publicly manageable.
James describes desire’s progression through temptation and conception to mature sin and death; therefore the church must evaluate not only a compromise’s small beginning but its end.

Application: identify the small compromise, moved boundary, dismissed conviction, or fed appetite; bring it to the Lord and to those harmed, trusting God’s promise to forgive and purify confessing sinners.

documents.excerpt: Josh opens with a common objection to Christianity: its commands can look like an exhausting list of prohibitions and an impossible demand for perfection. His rapid examples include "Don’t have sex outside of marriage," "Don’t love money," "Love your enemies," "Love strangers," and "Honor marriage."
excerpts: Josh opens with a common objection to Christianity: its commands can look like an exhausting list of prohibitions and an impossible demand for perfection. His rapid examples include "Don’t have sex outside of marriage," "Don’t love money," "Love your enemies," "Love strangers," and "Honor marriage."
The gospel is not merely that Christ teaches better behavior; Christ gives new hearts so that forgiven sinners begin to love what he loves, finding joy and freedom in obedience.
God does not simply hand saved people a kingdom handbook: "He puts his spirit within them," gives them power, changes their desires, and enables a new life.
Josh says, "He writes his law on their hearts," so the order is grace and inward renewal before the commands that follow.

documents.excerpt: Kingdoms, presidents, elections, friends, churches, bodies, memories, and wealth change, but Jesus Christ remains the same forever.
excerpts: Kingdoms, presidents, elections, friends, churches, bodies, memories, and wealth change, but Jesus Christ remains the same forever.
The Jesus who sat by the fire and "forgave Peter for denying him still forgives today."
The Jesus who told the dying thief he would be "in paradise that day" still welcomes sinners, even as Josh notes that the thief had no time for baptism or a polished doctrinal statement.
The Jesus who appeared behind locked doors to "doubting Thomas" still turns doubt into belief.
The Jesus who "called Lazarus from the grave" still gives life to the dead.
His promise remains: "All whom the Father gives me will come to me and whoever comes to me I will never drive away." Because Jesus does not change, neither do his promises.

documents.excerpt: Josh thanks the Father for Scripture, Hebrews, and the supremacy of Jesus from beginning to end.
excerpts: Josh thanks the Father for Scripture, Hebrews, and the supremacy of Jesus from beginning to end.
He thanks Jesus for "humbling yourself, taking our flesh," living the life sinners could not live, dying the death they deserved, and taking their place.
Addressing the crucified King, he prays, "All things were made through you and for you," yet the creation mocked its maker.

Josh recalls the mockery, "You can save others. Why can’t you save yourself?" and says Jesus stayed on the cross because he saw "this joy"—a redeemed family of faith called to trust, serve, love, and change the world.

He asks the Lord for needed power, help to forgive others and themselves, and grace to walk faithfully; he closes by thanking God for the series, Jesus, and the cross, then prays in Jesus’ name, "Amen."

excerpts: Enoch shows faith walking with God amid wickedness; prayer, meditation, fasting, Scripture, worship, serving others, and speaking God’s word all cultivate that walk.
Abel died for faith while Enoch never died, showing that God gives different assignments to those who trust him; mature faith responds, “God, you know what you’re doing.”
Noah shows faith working under social pressure: he picked up a hammer, obeyed, influenced his family, and prepared an ark.
Josh calls these earlier believers “the cloud of witnesses who went before us,” whose lives demonstrate faith in action.
Jesus later used the flood to warn people about his return; Josh presents the cross as Christ’s blood-soaked ark and urges listeners to enter before the door closes.

Faith can change circumstances, but it does not guarantee that God will do so.
